collections.name: Anderson Collection at Stanford University
collections.founder: Harry W. and Mary Margaret "Moo" Anderson (with Mary Patricia Anderson Pence)

profile.structure: Gift to a university; purpose-built building (a Stanford unit)
profile.publicAccess: Open to the public at Stanford, free
profile.currentState: At Stanford University since 2014, in a purpose-built building.

pathwayTimeline.event: 121 works pledged to Stanford
Purpose-built Ennead building opens (September 21)

collections.origin: The Andersons, a Bay Area family, built one of the foremost private collections of 20th-century American art over nearly 50 years, and gave it to Stanford as a university partnership rather than founding a standalone family museum.

collections.name: Colección Patricia Phelps de Cisneros

profile.structure: Private collection dispersed by gift into public museums; no founder museum
profile.publicAccess: Gifted works accessioned and shown at each recipient museum
profile.currentState: Works held in six museum collections, including MoMA's Cisneros Institute for the Study of Art from Latin America.
profile.size: ~340+ works gifted (2016 and 2018 tranches); full collection size unpublished

composition.focus: Latin American modern and contemporary art, with a geometric-abstraction core
recipients: Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía
Museo de Arte Moderno de Buenos Aires

pathwayTimeline.event: Collecting begins
~102 works gifted to MoMA, founding the Cisneros Institute for the Study of Art from Latin America
200+ works by 91 artists gifted to six museums across the Americas and Europe

collections.origin: Patricia and Gustavo Cisneros began collecting Latin American art in the 1970s, building one of the world's foremost holdings, with a core in mid-century geometric abstraction. Rather than found a museum, Patricia Phelps de Cisneros chose deliberate dispersal, gifting works into the permanent collections of major existing institutions so that Latin American art enters the global canon.

collections.name: Corcoran Gallery of Art

pathwayTimeline.event: Founded
Dissolved by court order (cy pres); collection distributed to the National Gallery of Art and other Washington institutions

collections.origin: The Corcoran Gallery of Art was founded in 1869 by William Wilson Corcoran, a Washington banker, to house his collection and support American art. It was among the earliest art museums in the United States and operated for most of its history as a private museum with an affiliated art school.

collections.name: Credit Suisse Art Collection (absorbed into the UBS Art Collection)

profile.structure: Corporate collection, absorbed into an acquirer's larger corporate collection
profile.publicAccess: Displayed inside bank offices; not a dedicated public venue
profile.currentState: Absorbed into the UBS Art Collection following UBS's 2023 emergency takeover of Credit Suisse; integration ongoing.
profile.size: ~13,500 works (absorbed); combined UBS collection 40,000+ works post-merger

composition.focus: Swiss contemporary art (Credit Suisse's holding); UBS's own collection is globally curated, blue-chip contemporary
selectedArtists: Monica Studer & Christoph van den Berg

pathwayTimeline.event: Credit Suisse begins a corporate art collection of Swiss contemporary art
Credit Suisse is absorbed into UBS in a state-brokered emergency merger; its ~13,500-work collection is absorbed into the UBS Art Collection

collections.origin: Credit Suisse built a corporate collection of Swiss contemporary art beginning in 1975, displayed across its bank offices. When Credit Suisse was absorbed into UBS in a 2023 emergency, government-brokered merger, its roughly 13,500-work collection was absorbed whole into UBS's own larger corporate collection, and the two banks' holdings are still being integrated.

collections.name: De la Cruz Collection

profile.structure: Free private museum (2009–2024); privately owned, no foundation
profile.publicAccess: Was free and open to the public, 2009–2024; now closed
profile.currentState: Museum closed 2024 after the founder's death; collection consigned to auction.

pathwayTimeline.event: Free 30,000-sq-ft private museum opens in Miami's Design District
Founder Rosa de la Cruz dies; museum closed and the collection consigned to Christie's (May 2024 sale, 25 works, ~$34M)

collections.origin: Rosa and Carlos de la Cruz built a contemporary art collection in Miami and opened it to the public as a free private museum in the Design District, a space also meant to support local artists.

collections.name: Deutsche Bank Collection / PalaisPopulaire
collections.founder: Deutsche Bank AG (corporate collection; initiated by executive board member Herbert Zapp)

profile.structure: Internal corporate art program (Deutsche Bank AG "Art & Culture" division)
profile.publicAccess: PalaisPopulaire open to the public in central Berlin through end of 2026, then rotating exhibitions at partner venues from 2027
profile.currentState: Closing its Berlin exhibition venue at the end of 2026; the collection continues on rotating loan to partner venues from 2027.
profile.size: ~55,000–57,000 works on paper and photographs (figure contested across sources)

composition.focus: Contemporary drawings, prints and photography, principally post-1945

pathwayTimeline.event: Deutsche Bank board member Herbert Zapp begins buying works on paper, seeded by 57 Beuys drawings
Collection formally established, anchored to the bank's 150th-anniversary narrative
PalaisPopulaire opens in the historic Prinzessinnenpalais, Unter den Linden, Berlin
~200 modern works sold to fund new acquisitions
PalaisPopulaire closure announced; lease not renewed; closing festival Nov 19-22, 2026
Collection continues via rotating exhibitions at partner venues; Artist of the Year award continues in a new roving format

collections.origin: In the late 1970s, Deutsche Bank executive Herbert Zapp began buying art for the bank, starting with 57 early drawings by Joseph Beuys. The collection grew into one of the largest corporate art collections in the world. In 2018 the bank opened PalaisPopulaire, a dedicated public exhibition venue in Berlin; in 2026 it announced the venue's closure at the end of the year, shifting from a fixed public building to a rotating-partnership model while keeping the collection intact.

collections.name: Fisher Collection at SFMOMA

profile.structure: Family-owned collection on long-term loan to a public museum
profile.publicAccess: On permanent public view in dedicated Fisher galleries at SFMOMA
profile.currentState: On 100-year loan to SFMOMA since 2009; dedicated galleries fully reinstalled in 2026.
profile.size: 1,100 works (720+ on the initial loan, by ~100 artists)

composition.focus: postwar and contemporary art (post-1960s American and European)

Planned Presidio museum dropped after community opposition
Collection placed on a 100-year renewable loan to SFMOMA, family retains ownership
Dedicated Fisher galleries open in SFMOMA's expansion
First full reinstallation since 2016

collections.origin: Gap Inc. co-founders Donald and Doris Fisher built one of the largest US private collections of modern and contemporary art, and chose to place it on long-term loan to a public museum rather than open a museum of their own.

collections.name: Las Vegas Museum of Art

profile.structure: Independent nonprofit museum, in partnership with LACMA
profile.publicAccess: Prelude venue (Grand Central Galleries) open; full museum planned fall 2029
profile.currentState: Under construction in Symphony Park; a prelude venue (Grand Central Galleries) opened 2026, full museum planned for fall 2029.
profile.size: n/a — no permanent collection of its own; access via a 50-year LACMA loan/curation partnership to LACMA's 150,000-object collection

composition.focus: General art museum (LACMA partnership, no announced sole curatorial thesis)

pathwayTimeline.event: An earlier Las Vegas branch effort (Art Museum at Symphony Park) merges into the Nevada Museum of Art rather than opening in Las Vegas
Elaine Wynn founds the Las Vegas Museum of Art as an independent nonprofit, with a LACMA partnership announced
Elaine Wynn dies (April); LVMA and LACMA continue the project without her
Grand Central Galleries prelude venue opens in Symphony Park
Full museum planned to open (delayed from an earlier fall 2028 target)

collections.origin: Elaine Wynn, Wynn Resorts co-founder and a longtime LACMA trustee, spent years pursuing a standalone art museum for Las Vegas after an earlier attempt folded into Nevada's existing museum in Reno. In 2024 she founded the Las Vegas Museum of Art as its own nonprofit, brokering a 50-year partnership giving it access to LACMA's collection. She died in April 2025, before the museum opened; the institution and its LACMA partnership are continuing under the board she built.

collections.name: Lucas Museum of Narrative Art

composition.focus: Narrative art — illustration, comic art, film, photography, and fine art

pathwayTimeline.event: Museum opens in Los Angeles

collections.origin: George Lucas's collecting began in college and grew, with Mellody Hobson, into a large collection organized around a single idea, that visual storytelling is a serious art. Rather than disperse it, they funded a purpose-built museum in Los Angeles to hold it, opening in 2026.

collections.name: The Barnes Foundation

profile.currentState: Operating in Philadelphia since 2012; relocated from Merion by court order.

composition.focus: Impressionist, Post-Impressionist, and early Modern painting, hung in fixed ensembles

pathwayTimeline.event: Chartered as an educational foundation in Merion
Relocated to Philadelphia by court order under cy pres

collections.origin: Albert C. Barnes assembled deep holdings of Impressionist, Post-Impressionist, and early Modern painting in the early twentieth century, and established an educational foundation, installing the works in fixed ensembles of his own arrangement. His trust set strict terms after his death, restricting whether works could be moved or loaned, how they were hung, and who could see them.

collections.name: The Broad Art Foundation

profile.structure: Private foundation lending library (and its own museum, The Broad, 2015)
profile.publicAccess: Loans to 550+ institutions worldwide; The Broad museum free to the public
profile.currentState: Active; a lending library since 1984, and The Broad museum (free) since 2015.

pathwayTimeline.event: Broad Art Foundation founded as a lending library
The Broad museum opens (free) in downtown Los Angeles

collections.origin: Eli and Edythe Broad built a large postwar and contemporary collection and made it public chiefly through a lending library, a deliberate alternative to warehousing art, lending thousands of works to museums worldwide, alongside a free museum of their own. The model has continued since Eli Broad's death in 2021.

collections.name: The Chinati Foundation

profile.publicAccess: Open by tour; annual October open house

composition.focus: Minimalism and related postwar and contemporary art

pathwayTimeline.event: Begins renovating the former Fort D.A. Russell, with Dia Art Foundation support
The Chinati Foundation is established
Donald Judd dies

collections.origin: Donald Judd, dissatisfied with how museums rotated art in and out of view, wanted permanent installation. In the 1970s he moved to Marfa and, with Dia Art Foundation support, made a permanent home for a small number of works on the site of a former army fort.

sections.heading: The installations
sections.body: Chinati holds large-scale work as permanent, unmovable ensembles rather than a rotating collection: Judd's own 100 works in mill aluminum and 15 in concrete, Dan Flavin's fluorescent installation across six former barracks, and John Chamberlain's sculptures downtown. Each work is installed in fixed relation to the buildings and the site.

sections.heading: After the founder
sections.body: Judd was the sole decision-maker, acquiring the land, siting every work, and setting the foundation's mission before his death in February 1994. It has operated in substantially its founded form since, through successive directors.

collections.name: The Klesch Collection

profile.structure: Private collection (no public venue); funds a university fellowship
profile.publicAccess: Not open to the public; works appear via loans and museum exhibitions
profile.currentState: Collection retained privately; funding a two-year postdoctoral fellowship at Birkbeck, University of London, from 2026.

pathwayTimeline.event: Collection begins with a set of Arcimboldo's Four Seasons
Klesches endow a two-year AI/art-history postdoctoral fellowship at Birkbeck, University of London

collections.origin: Gary and Anita Klesch began collecting Old Masters in 2014 with a set of paintings by Giuseppe Arcimboldo and built a private collection of 15th- to 17th-century European painting. Rather than founding a museum, they have funded scholarships and, in 2026, an academic fellowship connecting art history and artificial intelligence — putting the collection's resources into the field's scholarly infrastructure instead of a building.

decisions.label: Partner with an institution
decisions.framing: A collector does not have to found a new institution to keep a collection together and publicly accessible. It can be placed with one that already exists.
relevantWhen: They want the collection to stay publicly accessible.
They do not want to build and operate a museum.
An existing institution is a natural fit for what the collection contains.
They are willing to give up some ownership or some control.
They want institutional infrastructure for conservation, exhibitions, and public access.

values: A dedicated building at the university
University holds and shows the collection (both founders deceased)
None; galleries within the museum's own expansion
Governed by the documented loan terms
Loans to 550+ institutions; own free museum
The foundation, and later its own museum

questions: Does the collection have to remain together?
How long does the arrangement last?
Who pays for conservation, insurance, and installation?
How much control does the collector retain?
What happens after the collector dies?
Can either party end the arrangement?
sources: SFMOMA; the Doris and Donald Fisher Collection

topics.title: The Great Wealth Transfer and Art
topics.intro: Over the coming decades an unprecedented amount of private wealth will pass between generations. A large share of it is held by people who also own art, which puts the question of what becomes of a collection at the center of a much larger transition.

facts.label: Projected global wealth transfer over the coming decade (order of magnitude; sources and window vary)
Illustrative art-and-collectibles exposure implied under a modeled UHNW-share assumption — a Deloitte model, not a reported count
Share of inherited art that is retained rather than sold — the transition is usually about a change of hands, not a sale

sections.heading: The scale of the transition
sections.body: The wealth passing to heirs over the next decade is measured in tens of trillions of dollars, and a meaningful portion of it sits in art and collectibles. The headline figures are modeled estimates, not counts, and should be read as orders of magnitude.

sections.heading: Why ownership transition matters even without a sale
sections.body: Most inherited art is kept, not sold. That means the central event for a collection is usually a change of custody and responsibility, not a moment in the market, and it is exactly the moment that is most often unmanaged.

sections.heading: What it means for collections
sections.body: As collections change hands at scale, more families face the same set of decisions at once, with limited guidance on how others have handled them. That is the territory the Collection Index maps.

sources: Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting

topics.title: Estate Planning and Art Collections
topics.intro: Art does not move through an estate the way financial assets do. It is illiquid, taxed differently, expensive to hold, hard to divide, and often wanted by some heirs and not others. This is how that landscape works, and where it turns on professional advice.

facts.label: Federal estate & gift tax exemption per individual (2026)
Maximum federal rate on long-term gains from collectibles, vs 20% on most other assets, plus the 3.8% net investment income tax where it applies
Basis is generally stepped up to fair market value at death (IRC §1014)

sections.heading: What makes art different
sections.body: Illiquidity (a work cannot be partially sold to pay a tax bill), a higher collectibles capital-gains rate, estate-tax exposure at full value on an asset that produces no income, qualified-appraisal requirements, the cost of physical custody, and the problem that a single work cannot be divided among several heirs.

sections.heading: The decisions this forces
sections.body: Keep or sell; who receives the works; keep the collection intact or divide it; gift during life or transfer at death; give to charity and in what form; use a foundation or a trust.

sections.heading: The federal tax framework
sections.body: The 2026 federal estate and gift tax exemption is about $15M per individual with a 40% top rate; long-term gains on collectibles are taxed at a 28% federal maximum plus the 3.8% NIIT where applicable; and basis is generally stepped up to fair market value at death. Every figure here must be verified against the primary source before it is relied upon.

sections.heading: Charitable gifts of art
sections.body: A donor can generally deduct fair market value for a long-term-held work given to a public charity only if the charity's use is related to its exempt purpose (the related-use rule); deductions are capped as a share of adjusted gross income; and non-cash gifts above $5,000 require a qualified appraisal and IRS Form 8283, with high-value art reviewable by the IRS Art Advisory Panel.

sections.heading: State and other jurisdictions
sections.body: State estate and inheritance taxes vary by domicile and where works are held; a handful of states levy their own with far lower exemptions than the federal one, and other countries differ more sharply still. Specific jurisdiction pages will be added only where there is enough verified material to be useful.

sections.heading: Questions to work through
sections.body: Who legally owns the collection, and through what entity? What is the current cost basis? When was each work last appraised? Do the heirs want the collection? Would a museum accept it, and on what terms? Is the estate above or below the exemption? Gift during life or transfer at death?

sections.heading: Professional roles
sections.body: A qualified appraiser establishes value; an estate and tax attorney structures the transfer and models consequences; an accountant handles filings; an insurance specialist covers valuation, transport, and storage; an art adviser or collection manager assists with records, transactions, and institutional relationships.

sources: IRS, charitable contributions of property; Form 8283; Art Advisory Panel
